title: Modal perfect (double infinitive)
subtitle: Ik heb moeten werken: two infinitives instead of a participle

lessons.title: kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen in the perfect

explain.text: In the perfect, a modal verb that is followed by another verb does **not** get a participle. You use **hebben** and put **two infinitives** at the end (the *double infinitive*): *Ik heb gisteren **moeten werken**.* Not *gemoeten*.

The auxiliary is **always hebben** with a modal, even if the second verb normally takes *zijn*: *Ik heb naar huis moeten gaan.* The participles *gemoeten, gekund, gewild, gemogen* only appear when there is **no** second verb: *Dat heb ik niet gewild.* *Zij heeft het niet gekund.*

explain.en: We had to wait for a long time.

explain.nl: Hij heeft het niet kunnen vinden.
explain.en: He was not able to find it.

explain.text: In everyday speech the **simple past** (*Ik moest werken, Zij kon niet komen*) is just as common. The double infinitive is important because it is the correct form whenever you do use the perfect.

lessons.title: laten, zien, horen, gaan, komen, blijven

explain.text: A few more verbs work the same way when they are followed by an infinitive: **laten, zien, horen, helpen** take **hebben**, and **gaan, komen, blijven** take **zijn**. The participle is replaced by the infinitive: *Ik **heb** hem **zien komen**.* *Ik **ben** gaan zwemmen.*

head: verb
perfect example
rows: Ik heb mijn haar laten knippen.

explain.text: The same happens in the pluperfect: *Ik **had** mijn haar **laten knippen**.* *Zij **was** komen eten.*

explain.nl: Wij hebben onze auto laten repareren.
Zij is gisteren bij ons komen eten.
explain.en: She came to eat with us yesterday.

explain.text: With a real object only (no second verb) these verbs have normal participles: *Ik heb hem gezien*, *Ik ben gebleven*, *Ik heb het gehoord*.

lessons.title: Pluperfect with modals: had moeten, had kunnen

explain.text: With **had + modal infinitive** you say what you **should have** or **could have** done. It is very common to express regret or a mild reproach: *Ik **had** het **moeten weten**.* (I should have known.) *Je **had** eerder **kunnen bellen**.* (You could have called earlier.)
In questions the auxiliary comes first: *Heb je lang moeten wachten?* The infinitives stay together at the end.

explain.nl: Zij had willen komen, maar zij was ziek.
explain.en: She had wanted to come, but she was ill.

explain.nl: Dat had je eerder kunnen zeggen!
explain.en: You could have said that earlier!

explain.text: *Hij heeft kunnen komen* = he was able to come. *Hij had kunnen komen* = he could have come (but did not).
